title: History of Hindu-Christian Encounters, AD 304 to 1996
byline: by Sita Ram Goel · Voice of India · 1986, enlarged second edition 1996
lede: Christian historians have written many accounts of how missionaries saw Hinduism. Goel says he searched libraries in five countries in 1989 and found no account of how Hindus saw Christianity, so he wrote one. The book is a chronicle of encounters across seventeen centuries. Each is told from the Hindu side, from Sanskrit pandits answering a British civil servant in verse to Gandhi's half-century of argument with missionaries.

note: Goel writes as a fierce critic of Christianity, and the late chapters are openly abusive about the Church. This guide follows the history he narrates, attributed to him, and leaves out his invective.

sections.title: Seventeen centuries of encounters
sections.lede: Each entry is one of Goel's chapters. He calls the early contacts a “monologue”: Christians declaring and Hindus not answering. The dialogue begins around 1700, and in his view it was the Hindu side that improved.

sections.title: Who paid for India's missions, 1950–54
sections.lede: The Madhya Pradesh government's Christian Missionaries Enquiry Committee (the Niyogi Committee) traced ₹29.27 crore received from abroad in four and a half years. It concluded that most of it, though given for schools and hospitals, went on conversion work.
sections.note: From the committee's figures as reproduced in the book, in lakh rupees.
